author: claude
title: The Role of Rake and Curved Wingtips

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: If you look out the window on many airliners, the end of the wing turns upward. What are those shapes for?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: They're designed to reduce something called induced drag. When a wing creates lift, air with higher pressure under the wing tries to move to the lower pressure above it. At the wingtip, it curls around and forms a spinning vortex.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Like a small tornado behind each wing?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: More or less. That swirling air takes energy from the airplane. It's a kind of drag, which means more fuel is needed.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So the upturned tips stop that swirl?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: They make it weaker. On the Airbus A320 family, they're called sharklets. They're tall and curved, a bit like a shark's fin. Other types are winglets, with similar ideas.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: But the Boeing 787 doesn't have them, right?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Good observation. The 787 uses a raked wingtip. The wing gets thinner and sweeps back more strongly near the end. It reaches a similar goal, without a vertical piece.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: How much fuel does this save?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Usually a few percent, depending on the route. That doesn't sound like much. But for an airline flying thousands of flights, a few percent means a huge amount of fuel and money, and lower emissions too.
